Hi, I'm Misha. I'm a UI engineer at Netflix. My team builds tools for content analysis. To put it simply, we detect scary and grown up stuff - to make sure shows like Squid Game or Stranger Things are recommended to you - and not to your little kids.

These days, I also spend a lot of time on developer productivity - helping to increase AI adoption across Netflix teams.

But I'm not going to talk about AI today. Well… a bit.
Instead, I want to show you how our product team adopted Netflix UI platform tooling - with two real-life examples and learnings you can easily apply at your company.

To set some context, let me tell you about Netflix UI Platform. What’s that and why we need it?
Let’s imagine you’d like to watch something on Netflix. For example, Squid Game. Anyone here watched Squid Game? You search for it, you find it, there it is.

But, before a movie is ready to play, it goes through a long journey.
It starts with a screenplay. Then, deals are signed - with actors, directors, writers.
Financials are handled.
The movie is produced.
Promoted.
Localized.
Age rated.

And that's just the surface. There are hundreds of internal apps that power this process.

You’ve also probably heard a bit about Netflix culture. Iterate fast, run experiments, innovate, don’t let processes or bureaucracy stop you.

To be successful, the business needs to balance that off with quality, consistency, multi-platform support.
These two groups don’t always match.

Netflix's answer to that mismatch is platform tooling. Shared tools and libraries that help ship fast without sacrificing quality.

On the Web UI side, we call those UIPR. UI Paved Road.

Spoiler alert: that paved road has some bumps.

Why migrate to platform tooling at all?

Every codebase grows in complexity over time, right? But when you migrate to platform tooling... a big chunk of that complexity goes away. You're no longer maintaining custom solutions. Complexity and maintenance drop. Onboarding gets easier.

And everything else goes up: reliability, productivity, consistency, security. Because the platform team handles those concerns for you, across all apps.

Before UIPR and platform creation, every Netflix team picked tools that worked best for them. Which meant every team picked something different.

Here are all JS bundlers which were used across the apps. React-scripts, vite, webpack, gulp... has anyone here heard of craco/craco? Yeah.

And it wasn't just bundlers. Same story for styles, forms, table, localization.

How did the platform team go from 8 different bundlers to one paved road recommendation? Three phases.

First, analyze. Look at what hundreds of apps are using. What can be shared. What is app-specific.
Second, select. Explore the options, find what works best, document it, maintain it as a platform.
Third, bundle. Package everything into a single framework so teams can adopt it in one go.
UIPR stands on two pillars. Web Framework. Hawkins Design System.
The first pillar of UIPR. Web Framework. Let me show you what Web Framework adoption looked like for our team.

Here's a very simplified version of one of our apps. It has a movie search component and a user menu in the header.

From the architectural standpoint, it’s a monorepo app, which depends on two reusable packages: movie-search and user-menu.

Looks simple, right? It's not. Because it’s not using UIPR platform tools yet.

Instead, the app and packages depend on another package called Application Provider. It handles integration with internal system and provides common shared tools like a configured GraphQL client, feature flags, telemetry and more. Application Provider pulls those from other custom packages - all living in the same monorepo.

A monorepo of around 50 packages and 10 apps that our team owns.

On top of that, there is a community layer. Libraries for auth, logging, and more - maintained by entire Netflix Enterprise community. And each app has its own configs and code generation logic. That's the legacy setup we inherited.

If you look closer, a big chunk of this can be reused across apps. Most apps need the same things: auth, error handling, feature flags, telemetry. TypeScript, ESLint, and Vite default configs. So this must be provided by UIPR platform.

And it is. All of these indeed have UIPR equivalents now. We no longer need to maintain custom alternatives in our monorepo. The monorepo is much leaner.
Now, Application Provider can pull from platform directly.
And provide it all to our apps and packages.
But wait, if Application Provider is just an orchestrator of platform libs... it must be maintained by the platform, too. And that’s exactly how Web Framework was born.

Now our app just needs to plug into Web Framework entrypoint and get all the tooling out of the box. No more custom infrastructure packages cluttering the monorepo. The app just handles business logic - and nothing else.

So, Web Framework gives you this enterprise-ready pre-configured app setup out of the box. All of that managed by the platform team.

The platform team also keeps your dependencies up-to-date. And there is even a plugin system, in case you still need something custom.

Now you can see why Web Framework became the migration goal for Netflix's internal apps.
But our team was one of the first to migrate. So we had to figure out the process for that.

Our first approach: Big Bang Migration. Replace Application Provider with Web Framework, across all apps and packages at once.

Sounds great! Quick question for the room. Who's tried a big bang migration like this? … and succeeded? Yeah, so you probably know where this is going…

The app and packages all depend on Application Provider.
Then, just swap those dependencies to Web Framework, right?
But there's another app in the monorepo. It also pulls in Application Provider and the same re-usable packages. And you can't have both in the same monorepo. Web Framework and Application Provider conflict because they configure the same tools. So you need to migrate that app too.
And then the rest. You can’t migrate one app without migrating them all. It’s like a snowball.

And that’s the actual dependency graph of our monorepo at that point.
That little thing in the center is Application Provider.

During the big bang migration, the problems piled up.
Tight coupling - all apps and packages depend on the same things. You can't migrate one app without migrating all of them. And you can't verify everything works until everything is done.
Bugs everywhere - it’s impossible to reliably catch regressions across all apps.
Incompatible features - Vite, React Router and many other libs needed upgrades first, to meet web framework requirements.
Missing features - some very specific things Web Framework didn't cover at all.
Cross-team coordination - every team in the monorepo had to ship it’s part of the migration. And we couldn't finish until they all did.
Frequent rebasing - to stay in sync with dev.
And the cherry on top: a million-line diff. Impossible to review.
Big bang migration failed.

To be fair, it had some pros. You need to do it just once, and everyone benefits. It’s a focused effort you can track. And it highlighted all of the blockers we had.

But the bottom line: there's no room for error. One blocker stops everything, teams have to wait for each other, and regressions are hard to catch.

We cancelled it.

Instead, we went with the second approach: phased migration. We split one big effort into three phases: preparation, the migration itself, and follow-ups. Also, we pinned dependencies per app, so Web Framework and Application Provider can temporarily co-exist in one monorepo. That solved dependency conflicts and unblocked migrating apps one-by-one.
Start with one pioneer app to figure out the process and estimate effort. Then replicate it to the second one. Then the next, And if one fails, it doesn't block the rest.

With this approach, there is much more green than red.

You get flexibility, white-glove platform support, and each step is small enough to review and verify. The pioneer app becomes a blueprint for everyone else.

Of course, it has some tradeoffs, too. Some apps lag behind, and the monorepo is a bit messy until every team completes the migration - multiple versions of the same library are pulled in.

We decided: that’s the way to go.

Here's the phased approach in practice. If you can’t see everything here from where you’re sitting, that’s exactly the point. Instead of one massive effort, we now have this long list of small, independent tasks. Same runbook for every app. Each phase (preparation, migration, follow-ups) can be done separately, with items parallelized, and verified on their own.

And once you've documented this process for one app: this high-level plan, the step-by-step guides, the PRs. You can hand that runbook to your most hardworking teammate.
The one that never complains about rebasing.

Some outcomes of the phased approach.

We went from two months for the pioneer app migration to under a week for every app after it. The reason is how well we documented the process, and how easy it was to follow.
In fact, we turned those docs and artifacts into an agent skill - so an AI agent can run the migration end-to-end.
The docs and the skill turned out useful not just for our monorepo, but for many others across the company.

What we learned from the process:

Divide and conquer. Big bang failed under its own weight. So, it’s better to ship one small item at a time.
Fail fast, adapt faster. Big bang failed, but it exposed every blocker, and helped to shape approach #2.
Collaborate with the platform. We gave early feedback. Bugs got fixed before anyone else hit them. Our edge cases shaped the framework for everyone.
Leave a runbook. Step-by-step guides. Decision log. Pull requests. So that everyone can follow that runbook. Not just humans.
Now the second pillar of UI Paved Road: Hawkins - Netflix in-house design system.
Hawkins is the building blocks: components, forms, tables, guidelines, usage metrics. All built with performance, accessibility, and consistency in mind.

One of the challenges we faced with Hawkins, was the new table component adoption. Here's a table inside one of our apps.

It’s implemented using hawkins-table component. Which is built on top of a third-party library: React Data Grid.
By the way, raise your hand if you've heard of React Data Grid. [if few hands]: "A few of you." [if many hands]: "Oh, more than I expected. Veteran crowd."

Now, raise your hand if you've heard of AG Grid. [if many]: "Many more. Right." [if few]: "Niche crowd today."
AG Grid is one of the most popular JS table libraries. It has more features, better performance. So hawkins team selected it as the foundation for the next version of the table component. They're calling the component hawkins-table-next.

But there's a catch. It's not released yet. Still under development.

So, as a product team, how do we ship new features then? We need to make a decision: use the old table component, ship features now.
Or wait for the new table component, and ship features later.
Old table: no delay, familiar APIs. But you're knowingly creating tech debt.
New table: has more features, no tech debt. But it delays product work. And there's a learning curve.

Team Old Table raise your hand.
Now, Team New Table, raise your hand.

Neither option is great. So we found a third way.

Step one: use AG Grid directly. Don't wait for hawkins-table-next, start building with AG Grid APIs now. Ship product work on time.

Step two: Swap with hawkins-table-next once it’s released. Since it wraps AG Grid under the hood, you're already using the right APIs. The swap is minimal.

Step three: gradually migrate the other tables across the app. Until you have no references to the old table.

We call this approach “forward-adopt”.

The wins: no delay in product work, less tech debt to clean up later, and you get early feedback on new APIs. You catch missing features and regressions before the official release. And when table-next ships, the swap is easy because the APIs are already similar.

The trade-offs: there's a learning curve upfront, you need some initial styling and licencing workarounds, and there's cleanup after the final swap. But compared to the alternatives - it's a much better position.

What we learned from the process:

Align direction, not timing. You can't always wait for the platform. But if you're moving the same way, you'll eventually meet at one point.
Product work is non-negotiable. Your stakeholders should never care about such migrations. Product work must be delivered on time. That's what keeps you trusted to make such decisions in the future.
Give early feedback. Our feedback shaped table-next. With this migration, we were also helping build the final solution.

So next time you're waiting for the perfect tool to drop, start with what you have. Align early. Pave the road yourself.
